title: Spain election: Sanchez stood up against Trump. His own voters may be about to bring him down | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

For much of the past few years, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has enjoyed the kind of international reputation that few politicians do.

A staunch supporter of Ukraine and vocal advocate for Palestinian rights, Sánchez, 54, has positioned himself as a moral compass for progressives in Europe.

And while some European leaders compromised and sought to curry favor with US President Donald Trump in his second term, Sánchezchose defiance.

“We don’t want anything to do with Spain,” Trump said on March 3, after Madrid denied Washington use of its jointly operated bases for direct strikes on Iran, one ofmany disagreementsbetween the two NATO allies. The Spanish leader also rejected the White House’s demand that members of the alliance increase defense spending to 5% of GDP, prompting further criticism.

The attacks burnished Sánchez’s status in Europe as the torchbearer for a new strategy for dealing with Trump. But at home, the view has, for some time, been strikingly different on a broader range of matters.

After eight years in power, the corruption scandals embroilingthose around him, the migrant disaster in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, twocatastrophic train crashes, ahousing affordability crisisand, last but not least, an economy that though booming on paper continues not to deliver for ordinary people, the fatigue among Spaniards is palpable.

The last few months of his premiership have been plagued by successive strikes involving teachers, medical staff, rail workers and others, who say their living standards have been in decline. It was the failure to pass emergency measures to curb the housing crisis that finally brought down Sánchez’s coalition, prompting him to call a snap election last month.

As voters prepare to cast their ballots on Sunday, most opinion polls have Sánchez and his center-left Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) trailing behind the center-right People’s Party (PP). A charismatic and clever operator on the campaign trail, with a history as a political survivor who has consistently defied the odds, Sánchez has been able to reduce the gap between his party and PP in recent weeks.

Yet, even if he finishes ahead, most polls suggest it is highly unlikely PSOE and the other parties on the left will be able to secure enough votes to prevent a right-wing majority and a widely anticipated governing coalition between PP and the far-right Vox party.

If this happens, it’ll be the first time since the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975 and the instalment of a democratic system that the far right has been part of a Spanish government.

PP’s Alberto Núñez Feijóo – Sánchez’s main opponent – has run on a platform to right what he sees as the wrongs of the past eight years. His campaign ads and billboards across Spain read “the necessary change,” or “the necessary president.”

In effect, Feijóo, 65, is selling competence and rigor, in contrast to the chaos and spectacle he says has been the defining trait of the PSOE over the past few years: that is, something Spaniards may not necessarily desire but actually need.

“I’m not running to entertain Spain,” he said during an interview with Spanish newspaper La Razón on November 4. “I’m running to serve Spain.”

PP has taken aim at many of the crises they say have been the hallmark of PSOE’s rule. Chief among them are the two high-speed rail crashes this year, which killed 115 people and injured more than 300 others in total.

“You have managed the high-speed rail network with persistent negligence,” Feijóo told Sánchez during a head-to-head televised debate last week, accusing the Spanish prime minister and his government of not taking action despite repeated warnings and safety failures. Sánchez has promised to investigate and address problems.

Feijóo and the PP have criticized PSOE’s handling of and lack of accountability for an April 2025 blackout that left Spain without electricity for nearly 16 hours. They’ve also attacked what Feijóo calls an open-door policy on migration, blaming it for an increase in migrant boat crossings that has overwhelmed public services in Spain’s Canary Islands, off northwest Africa, as well as the deadly surge of migrants into Ceuta in July.

Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, has put migration front and center of its campaign, defending what it calls a “remigration” policy for irregular immigrants while blaming them for a rise in crime and accusing them of draining resources meant for Spaniards.

Neither of those claims is supported by official Spanish data, but Vox’s message has resonated, putting the radical party in prime position to potentially join a governing coalition after November 29.

When Sánchez became prime minister in 2018, he did so after unseating former PP leader Mariano Rajoy, whose government was engulfed by a series of corruption scandals.

As he called for a vote of no confidence in Rajoy’s government in parliament, Sánchez said the country needed a “democratic regeneration,” one that would restore people’s faith in the country’s institutions. But since assuming the premiership, his own inner circle has been plagued by allegations of graft.

In June, his former transport minister and right-hand man José Luis Ábalos was sentenced to 24 years in prison, convicted on corruption charges and accused of taking kickbacks from the purchase of facemasks during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The previous month, the PSOE headquarters in Madrid was raided by police as authorities investigated several of Sánchez’s close allies, including former Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, who’s denied wrongdoing.

Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, has also been ordered to stand trial over alleged influence peddling and misappropriation of public funds, charges she denies. His brother, David, was convicted in July of administrative misconduct but cleared of influence peddling.

Sánchez said he “never knew” of his former minister’s practices and vowed the government’s full cooperation, adding there can be no “room for impunity.”

At the same time, he’s portrayed accusations against his wife as politically motivated persecution.

In an interview with CNN’s Chief International Anchor Christiane Amanpour in September, he argued he and his government had been “very tough” on corruption but claimed “other cases” were “maneuvers from the opposition” to try to force him out.

Sánchez has never been named in any of the corruption scandals and has consistently denied any wrongdoing. Yet Spain’s far right has been able to paint a different picture, on this and other issues, through messaging heavily amplified on social media

The initial investigation into Sanchez’s wife originated from a legal complaint – based on media reports, some of which later turned out to be false – by a small civil servants’ union called Manos Limpias, or Clean Hands, which has ties to the far right. Vox later applied to join the proceedings through a Spanish legal mechanism that allows third parties to participate in criminal prosecutions.

Spanish courts have allowed the key allegations to proceed but this example illustrates how Vox and others on Spain’s political fringes have been able to transform these controversies into a broader indictment of Sánchez and his government.

Sánchez has repeatedly reminded Spanish voters he’s presided over a period of rapid and sustained economic growth.

Over the past few years, Spain’s economy has been one of the fastest growing in Europe, outpacing the likes of Germany, France, Italy or the United Kingdom, and the economic argument is usually a strong one: Decades of research show voters tend to reward incumbents with a strong performance on the economy.

Since 2018, Spain has seen overall unemployment fall from 15% to 10%, and youth unemployment shrink from 34% to 22%. The monthly minimum wage has also risen from €735 ($806) to €1,221 ($1,230), a 66% increase.

But the cost of living has also increased. The median wage has risen at a much slower pace than the minimum and, after inflation, the average worker’s purchasing power has remained largely unchanged.

Critics also argue the government has failed to capitalize on the economic boom to improve public services and people’s access to affordable housing.

Rents across Spain are now 44% higher than they were when Sánchez first came into office, according to property portal Idealista, and many Spaniards are being priced out of the cities they grew up in.

In 2023, when he narrowly won re-election, Sánchez promised to add 184,000 homes to the country’s affordable housing portfolio but, having failed to pass a budget for the past three years, his government has fallen well short. Independent factcheckers say he’s only delivered around 40,000 protected homes.

As he announced snap elections on October 5, the Spanish prime minister acknowledged his government had made mistakes and had not been able to deliver on all its promises, blaming a confrontational parliament and a frail coalition.

“If we are to do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people,” he said, asking for a bigger mandate and more time. “Many injustices still need to be corrected. There are still many social goals to achieve.”

After eight years at the helm, Spain’s great political survivor may struggle to convince the country to trust him with it again.
